## Why Compound leads

Compound is an AI analyst for finance: it builds Excel models, PowerPoint decks and memos from a firmâs own files. The scores reported here are for the product as it ships, the same agent customers use. Two factors account for most of its lead.

Better tools for Office files. Compound runs on its own rewrite of Excel, PowerPoint and Word : a spreadsheet engine that recalculates workbooks, and a document engine that draws slides the way PowerPoint does. A Compound agent builds native charts with their data embedded, including the newer types such as waterfall and box and whisker; ties the figures on each slide to the live model; and looks at a render of every page before it hands the deck over.

Models from more than one lab. Compound is not tied to a single model. Its harness routes each part of a task to the model that performs it best for the cost, across labs, and combines the results into one deliverable. A single-lab agent can choose only among its own labâs models; drawing on several lets Compound reach points on the cost chart that no single-lab agent reaches.

## What makes a strong IC deck

At most private equity firms, the final deliverable to the investment committee is a long deck, typically 50 to 100 pages. We built realistic data room tasks around the work that produces that deck: the diligence and the valuation model behind it. We grade each deck against the standard a senior partner applies before a deck goes to committee:

It leads with the answer. The price and the recommendation come first, followed by a bridge from the sellerâs number to ours.

Every figure ties. A number in the deck matches the model behind it and traces back to a document in the data room.

It makes a call when the documents disagree. The CIM, the monthly accounts and the quality of earnings report often conflict. The analyst reconciles them and states which figure to rely on.

It shows evidence in professional language. No icon cards with one-line blurbs, no conversational headings (âWhat we pay for itâ), no stock AI phrasing (âunlockâ, âmission-criticalâ), and no explanations of EBITDA to a committee. Each source names a document a reader can find.

### Halberd IC deck: describing the business

It follows the firmâs template. Layouts, fonts, colors and chart styles match the firmâs own.

Charts are native PowerPoint charts with their data embedded. A reader should be able to open a chart and see the numbers behind it. The example below shows the same Kilnmere EBITDA bridge from three agents. Compoundâs is a native waterfall chart. Claude Codeâs looks correct but is built from ten rectangles placed by hand. Codex CLIâs is a table, with every figure to four decimal places.

### Kilnmere IC deck: the EBITDA bridge

Updates leave no stale figures. A revised price or a new document is reflected on every page it affects.

Every comment is resolved. Each partner comment is either applied or answered with a reason.

The file opens cleanly. PowerPoint opens the deck without a repair prompt.

## Task design

The tasks cover three kinds of PowerPoint work: building a deck from a raw data room, building on a firmâs template, and editing an existing deck.

Investment committee deck. This is the core task. The agent receives a data room of more than a hundred documents and builds the investment committee deck, together with the valuation model in four of the six tasks. Judgment matters most here: which earnings to underwrite, which of the sellerâs adjustments to accept, what the business is worth, and which findings to raise. The model supplies the numbers; the deck carries the argument.

Bid. The agent recommends what to offer for a business and where to walk away, against a fund mandate the prompt sets out: a return target, a holding period and no reliance on multiple expansion. The bid in the deck has to tie to the return the model shows at that bid.

Lender and first-look decks. The same kind of data room, written for a different reader. In one task the agent writes the presentation to the companyâs lenders before signing, setting out what the deal needs from each. In another it writes a first-look deck for a Monday deal meeting: whether to submit a first-round bid, and in what range.

Deck on the firmâs template. The agent builds an investment committee deck from a data room on one of two fictional firmsâ templates (described below). In addition to everything we check on any IC deck, the new pages must look like the firmâs own.

Single exhibits. One data-heavy page built from a workbook: a market map, a valuation football field, or a peer margin comparison. PowerPoint has no native chart type for a market map or a football field, so the agent must construct them. Each page is judged on whether it makes its point at a glance: the size and share of each segment, the valuation ranges against the offer price, and the company clearly distinguished from its peers.

Updates. The agent receives an investment committee deck and its model, along with new information: the minutes of the committee meeting, a lenderâs term sheet received that morning, or documents added to the data room after the deck was written. It must update the model, carry the change through every page it affects, and leave the other pages unchanged.

Deck review. The agent receives a finished deck and its model before they go to the committee. In one task it reviews both and corrects every error, without changing figures that were already correct. In the other, the deal partner has left comments on the pages and sent a short email; the agent resolves the comments and drafts a reply to the partner.

Edits to existing decks. Real decks are rarely clean. The agent makes one routine edit to a deliberately difficult deck (described below): correcting a misspelled name, rolling figures forward a quarter, rebuilding a table pasted in as a picture, or retitling pages. Each edit contains a trap, such as a near-match that should not be changed. The task passes only if the edit is correct, nothing else changed, and PowerPoint opens the file cleanly.

Native charts. Thirty-six single-slide tasks, each asking for one native PowerPoint chart type or feature: every chart type PowerPoint offers except the region map, and features such as trendlines, error bars, logarithmic scales and secondary axes. A few edit an existing chart, and four leave the choice of chart to the agent.
